units.translation: b. Dionysius of Miletus in the first book of his Argonautica (see scholion a) says that Circe was the daughter of Aeetes and Hecate, the daughter of Perses, and the sister of Medea. For he says that two sons were born to Helios in those regions, whose names were Perses and Aeetes; these two took possession of the land, and Aeetes ruled over the Colchians and Maeotians, while Perses ruled over the Tauric region. Perses, being the elder, married a certain native woman, and a daughter was born to him, whose name was Hecate, who is said to have been manly in hunting and the first to discover deadly roots and to kill her own father with drugs. She was sent to Colchis and married Aeetes, her paternal uncle, and from her were born Circe and Medea. Circe, being older than Medea, surpassed her own mother, partly by hearing about many terrible things and partly by discovering them herself. Hesiod says that Circe was the daughter of Helios in these verses (Theog. 1011 ff.): 'Circe, daughter of Helios, son of Hyperion, bore to steadfast Odysseus in love Agrius and Latinus, blameless and strong.'

202-09 a. 'of whom even on the highest': because it is not lawful for the Colchians either to burn or bury male bodies, but wrapping them in fresh hides they hung the bodies of males, while the females they gave to the earth, as Nymphodorus says (fg 17 M. II 380), whom he followed. They worship especially Uranus and Earth.
